newsitem.title: GERMANY: European bulls run after Wall Street surge.
newsitem.headline: European bulls run after Wall Street surge.

text.p: European equity markets shook off single currency anxiety to advance to new highs on Friday, taking their lead from an overnight Wall Street surge and with little evidence of vertigo at these new dizzy heights.

An overnight rally on the Dow Jones Industrial index of U.S. stocks underpinned upbeat trading sentiment across Europe, while hopes of a ratification of a European stability pact at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam also lifted spirits.
By midday most indices had stabilised at higher levels.
* Germany's DAX-30 index hit a new record at 3,751.26 points in early bourse trade.
* France's CAC-40 index was up 0.9 percent at 2,785.18 points around midday, having earlier hit an all-time high at 2,805.37 points.
* The FTSE 100 index in London hit an all-time high of 4,796 points, before falling back slightly to 4,780.2 points.
* The IBEX-35 index in Madrid stood at 6,689.57 points, up 0.25 percent mid-morning, off record high of 6,743.33 points.
* Swiss shares also hit record at 5,396.5 points, with the SMI index up 14.9 points at 5,379.1.
* Dutch shares advanced to a high of 848.29 points early on, before settling back to 843.21 points, up 3.85.

European stocks have been hit by worries in recent days that a stability pact, aimed at ensuring fiscal discipline among EMU members after currency union kicks off on January 1, 1999, may not be ratified.

Central to these fears were worries that the newly-elected French government might try to stymie the stability pact. But French market players said calls by the Socialist government for a "social charter" attached to the pact were not such a bad idea, as unemployment was a destabilising factor.

Comments late on Thursday by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer signalling that sustainability, not precise figures, were of primary importance for a successful single currency, contributed to euro optimism on German markets.

"There is more confidence out there that the euro will come on time, even if it's weaker than expected, so people now expect that money will keep coming into Europe after currency union," said Jochen Waiblinger, assistant vice president of the Institutional Investors department at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.

With jitters about the future of the European economic and currency union (EMU) soothed, for the time being at least, European markets were able to give their full attention to catching up on the greatest bull run in Wall Street's history.
The Dow has risen around 1,250 points since the start of the year, and advanced 1.79 percent to 7,711.47 points on Thursday after weaker-than-expected U.S. retail sales figures.
Such massive gains have prompted some fears that the market may be overextended, creating a "bubble" just waiting to burst.
"People are really only mildly optimistic, not euphoric and there is a lot of fear around, which is a good insurance policy against a bubble," said Waiblinger.

Analysts said there was a reassuring background of moderate growth in Europe, low inflation and interest rates and continent-wide corporate restructuring programmes, which should detract from a crash scenario.
With interest rates so low, institutional investors remain bullish on European equity markets and a massive influx of funds is helping keep liquidity levels buoyant.
With European indices trading at such levels, some valuations of stocks are exaggerated, which means a bout of profit-taking cannot be ruled out in the mid-term.
But analysts in individual countries expect the bulls to keep running for the time being.
ABN Amro said in a report to clients that the outlook for the DAX index reaching 3,800 points looks "increasingly conservative" based on the market's recent heady surge.
French traders are confident that the CAC index will hit 3,000 points by the end of the year, while Amsterdam dealers see the market hitting 850 initially, advancing to 875 points.
